12.1b — Grid/Symmetry Jam: Build Day 1

Core-loop day again (10.1b rules, grid edition): by the end of class, a board exists in DATA, one move works end to end, and the win/lose stub prints. The one new idea today is the data structure that runs half the games ever made: a 2D array.

Build Day ~50 min

Step 1 — the board as data (list of lists):

const int W = 8; const int H = 8;
private int[,] grid = new int[W, H];       // 0 = empty, 1 = player, 2 = wall...

// or the AP way — a list OF lists:
// grid[ROW][COL] — the exam writes aList[r][c] exactly like this

Print the whole grid to the console each frame for now — Debug.Log row by row. You must be able to READ your board in text before you can trust it in sprites.

Step 2 — one move. The player cursor at (x, y): W/S/A/D changes it by ±1 — but ONLY inside the array's bounds. The two bugs of every grid game, met now:

int nx = x + dx;
int ny = y + dy;
if (nx >= 0 && nx < W && ny >= 0 && ny < H)  // BOUNDS — always
{
    x = nx;
    y = ny;
}

Step 3 — the symmetry hook. Whatever your pitch promised, wire the CHEAPEST version of it today: mirror the cursor on the other half (x2 = W - 1 - x — one line!), or spawn the enemy AI at the mirrored start. That one line IS the design; everything else elaborates it.

Step 4 — lose/win stub. Touch a hazard cell → print "lose"; reach the far cell → print "win". The loop exists even if nothing is drawn.

Bug Hunt: Grid classics

  1. You mixed x/y and row/col. Why is grid[y, x] the CONVENTION (row first) — and what does a swap look like on screen (a square board LIES — it looks correct!)? Test on a RECTANGLE.
  2. Off-by-one at the edge: W or W-1 for the last column? (11.4a's wrong-answer tell, costing you a day — count from 0.)
  3. The mirrored cursor walks off the opposite edge (you bounded one side, not the mirror). Which LINE bounds the mirror — and why did the cheap-symmetry trick not save you HERE?
Close of Day ~5 min

Tinker: Loop proof

  1. Console-drawn board + one working move + win/lose print. Commit + push: "12.1b: grid core".
  2. Sticky note: tomorrow's riskiest thing (10.1c ritual — it works; keep it).

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Build and PRINT a grid; explain grid[y, x] row-first
  • Move a cursor with bounds checks on both sides
  • Wire the cheapest version of your symmetry in one line
  • End the day with the loop running in text
